b: In the hands of any director besides Hamaguchi Ryūsuke, an extended scene in which a character stands in front of a whiteboard to diagram how capitalism functions might be the height of didacticism. Yet in his latest film, All of a Sudden, this sequence proves to be more than just a convenient mechanism for delivering sociopolitical context. For all the matter-of-fact delivery that Hamaguchi typically elicits from his performers, the moment is laden with emotion, as we watch the dying Mari (Okamoto Tao) make sense of the world she will soon leave and observe how empathetically nursing-home director Marie-Lou (Virginie Efira) listens.

With the help of French co-writer Léa Le Dimna, Hamaguchi extrapolates his tender drama from the correspondence between philosopher Miyano Makiko and anthropologist Isono Maho that was collected in the book When Life Suddenly Takes a Turn. Mari and Marie-Lou’s bond follows much the same arc as that of Miyano and Isono, whose relationship deepened after the former’s cancer took a turn for the worse. Yet many other elements and events that transpire with the characters in All of a Sudden derive from Hamaguchi’s own research and imagination.

Given the role that chance and risk play in bringing Marie-Lou and Mari together, the film could just as well bear the title of Hamaguchi’s 2021 film Wheel of Fortune and Fantasy. Marie-Lou, the director of a for-profit nursing home in the suburbs of Paris, struggles to sell her staff on implementing a new system of care known as Humanitude. Amid these training woes, she encounters Mari, a Japanese theater director presenting her work in the City of Lights. Both women know how to speak the other’s language, which opens up further pathways for unexpected and heartfelt connection. The relationship that develops transforms them both and radiates a restorative energy to all in their vicinity.

I spoke with Hamaguchi while he was in New York ahead of All of a Sudden’s theatrical release. Our conversation covered how his exposure to multilingual settings affected his approach to translation in the film, what he learned about his process from working outside his native Japan, and where he sees parallels between Humanitude and his own directing style.

That first conversation between Mari and Marie-Lou, where they discuss the ability to recognize when something important is being shared even when you don’t know every word, made me think about encounters like this one. Have interviews like these, and other settings where you speak with the aid of a translator, inspired your approach to language in All of a Sudden?

I have a particular interest in the voice, and that comes from my directing style. I have my actors do flat readings of the dialogue in the script, and that allows them to listen to the communicative qualities of just the voice and develop trust in what the voice is able to communicate. And I think that may be influenced a lot by the multilingual environments that I often find myself in. For about 10 years now, I’ve been attending film festivals, and I’ve also had opportunities to live abroad for periods of time. And, as you can see here, I understand quite a bit of English, but I always respond in Japanese. I think that itself is quite strange. People often think, “Well, if you can listen to and understand English, then why don’t you also answer in English?” But trying to restructure all of the ideas that I have in Japanese into the English language would just be too difficult for me, and that’s why I speak in Japanese. That connects to this idea of there being less of a block and more of an ease when you speak in your mother tongue. However, the idea that [the mother tongue] is the closest to the truth is maybe not completely true, because we see toward the end of the film that there are also things happening that negate that idea.

You understand English far better than I understand Japanese, but these settings are interesting because I hear everything you say twice: first in Japanese, where I pick up on the emotion, and then in English, where I get the information. Does something similar happen for you in that process?
If anything, with this experience of having to hear what I say twice, I wish that didn’t have to be. I wish I could speak directly. Maybe that frustration is a little bit in the film!

Some filmmakers use different-colored subtitles to indicate when multiple languages are being spoken, but I really loved that there was no distinction between the French and Japanese subtitles in the version for English-speaking audiences. What went into that decision?

We had the idea of displaying the two languages in different styles of subtitles, but the characters actually move between languages so fluidly and quickly that it would end up looking like the subtitles were flashing. If they were flashing white and yellow, or even if we just italicized one of the languages, it would create a distraction. I thought that French and Japanese are such different languages that if you’re watching the film and more or less attentively listening, you could differentiate between the two. But I’m also open to the idea that there could be confusion as to what language they’re actually speaking.
There was less confusion on my part about what language they were speaking and more that I just stopped actively paying attention!
That’s something that I hoped would happen as well. It’s all about highlighting the emotional connection that the two of them have and making sure that’s conveyed to the audience.

Do you feel a connection between Marie-Lou’s practice of Humanitude and your own filmmaking style? The method’s emphasis on seeing individuals in the fullness of their humanity is something I’d associate with your work.

Of course, there are many hints of my directing in the practice of Humanitude, an actual care practice that addresses patients with dementia by trying to accommodate the cognitive decline they’re experiencing. That allows them to be less fearful and limits resistance from the patients themselves. I thought that made a lot of sense. People with dementia are unable to see or hear as well [as they used to]. By accommodating that, caretakers can alleviate the fear that they experience, and that makes sure that they don’t resist the caretakers.

I think that act of accommodating people connects greatly to my directing style. At its core, Humanitude is about alleviating fear, and I actually started to see the connection after I made Happy Hour, a film where the actors were all people without acting experience. What’s needed in working with non-actors is to provide them with a kind of psychological safety. For instance, if they start to feel self-conscious about whether their performance is good or bad, that very quickly becomes unbearable. It was important for me to convey to them that their humanity, their true selves, were what was alluring. If they can express that in some way, that’s completely enough. All you have to do is remember the lines and do the movements that I tell you to do. And if that elicits a kind of emotion or even joy out of you, that’s great as well. But [my] baseline is to say that the actors themselves, as people, are completely sufficient.

I think that directors are thought of as people who pass judgment, but I think of the director as a person who provides support. Being able to communicate that to the actors is important. That stance is close to the principles of Humanitude. While that idea was directed toward non-actors, I felt that this was a helpful practice or concept to apply to professional actors as well.

Your co-writer, Léa Le Dimna, was by your side on the set of All of a Sudden as an interpreter. Did that affect the way you thought about the nature of directing, almost mirroring the film’s structure of mutual support and relying on the care of others to have your humanity affirmed?

I think that the work of a director is creating opportunities to be supported. I couldn’t have made this film without Léa Le Dimna, and I think her work was very similar to what I do with my actors, in the sense that she supported me in letting me be me. She lives in France and understands the country’s cultural background, and she was able to translate the dialogue in the script into that context.

When the pigeon poops on the characters, I wrote in the script that they grab a tissue. But she quickly [stated] that French people don’t carry around tissues, so then we said, “Okay, maybe we need to write a handkerchief. But does that mean that they’re going to be carrying around this handkerchief with bird poop on it all day?” She was like, “Well, yes, I think that’s what would happen.” Her work was invaluable in allowing me to preserve what I wanted to express, but in a way that was appropriate to the French cultural context. She was also present during all of the script readings, and her role wasn’t to correct the performances or me, but to allow me to do the kind of work that I do in Japan to the best of my ability in this different context.

How did you conceive of the connection between theater and acting, which are also seen in the film, and Humanitude? I know some disciplines have formalized a practice of drama therapy, and I’m not sure if you see the connection quite so literally, but it does feel of a piece with the care provided at Marie-Lou’s facility.

The connection between Humanitude and the source material that this film and its central relationship are based on is unclear. What I found in Humanitude is the idea that you see a person in the totality of their humanity, and you don’t try to define roles for people. Let’s say there’s a cancer patient and a doctor: Their relationship becomes a contractual one, between one who is ill and one who is providing care. There’s this idea that people’s relationships are created through these defined roles. Certainly, in an elder-care facility, the person with dementia is defined by having dementia and being the person who is being cared for. But, actually, they’re multifaceted human beings who have a totality of personhood that is often overlooked.

In the correspondence between the philosopher and the anthropologist that All of a Sudden is based on, the philosopher is the person who has cancer, but she’s not simply a person with cancer. She loves travel. She loves baseball. She loves her family. She’s a multifaceted human being. And what happens in their correspondence is that, midway, when she suddenly falls gravely ill, the dynamic isn’t reduced to one between an ill person and a healthy person. They’re interacting with each other as “I am me, you are you,” recognizing the totality of each other’s personhood. Humanitude has principles for practicing a kind of care, but there’s this idea that we use these care practices to activate the humanity that each person has within them.

I think that to participate in society, each one of us takes on a role. Those roles often require us to discard parts of our own humanity in order to maintain a functioning society. The truth is, I don’t know a lot about drama therapy, and I don’t know how acting connects to any kind of therapeutic effects. However, I think of acting as a way to make things that are socially unacceptable acceptable. For instance, if you begin acting without saying that you’re acting, that’s kind of terrifying. But if you stand on a stage and announce that you’re acting, then you’re able to take on a role or express things through it that wouldn’t otherwise be found socially acceptable. As long as acting doesn’t further corrupt a person, I see how there might be some therapeutic effects in acting out and expressing things that you otherwise couldn’t within a functioning society and under the social contract that we all live under.

I was struck by Mari’s words at the end of the film: “I want to live.” It hit me in the same place as the sign-language reading of Sonya’s final lines in Drive My Car: “We must live our lives.” Where that film frames living as an obligation, this one frames it as a desire. Does that shift reflect a change in your own outlook on life?

I think it’s that the story called for this type of line. For instance, at the end of the film, Mari couldn’t say something like, “I must live.” That wouldn’t feel right, so I don’t know if this is a reflection of my own changing perspective, that I went from a sense of obligation toward a will to live. Filmmakers are craftspeople. We take certain material and use it to make something, and then we present it to an audience. In Drive My Car, it was the situation of the two protagonists that defined how those lines play out. As for “I want to live,” I don’t think there are any lines from the actual source material that make their way into the film. However, it’s a sentiment that is very clearly present throughout the correspondence between those two women. It’s about heading toward death, but fundamentally, it’s about life. That’s what I wanted to convey.
